clue.text: Net gain-one wicket

definitions.meaning: what a fishing net brings in, a haul of fish
in cricket a batter can be out caught, one way of losing a wicket

explanation.definitionFit: A haul of fish is a catch, and a ball held by a fielder before it lands is a catch that takes a wicket.

clue.text: Packs boxes made of this material

definitions.text: Packs boxes made of this material

parts.words: Packs boxes made of this material
parts.note: packs of playing cards and the boxes they come in are both made of stiff paper board

explanation.definitionFit: Stiff pasteboard is used for playing cards and for packing boxes alike.

clue.text: Got in trouble with a beastly crossbreed

indicators.note: to trouble is to disturb, so the letters of the two short words are stirred up

explanation.surface: Someone has got into difficulties dealing with a hybrid animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A tigon is the hybrid offspring of a male tiger and a lioness, a crossbred beast.

clue.text: Last of three at bridge

parts.note: the Roman hero who, with two companions, held the bridge over the Tiber against the Etruscans and was the last to cross back

explanation.walkthrough: Macaulay's poem tells of three Romans holding the Sublicius bridge; the other two retreated first, leaving one alone. 'bridge' suggests the card game.
explanation.definitionFit: Horatius Cocles stayed on the bridge after his two comrades withdrew, the last of the three defenders.

clue.text: It's extremely woolly and suffers from the shakes

definitions.text: It's extremely woolly and suffers from the shakes

parts.words: It's extremely woolly and suffers from the shakes
parts.note: the extremity of a young sheep is woolly and wags constantly; the name is also given to the dangling catkins of hazel that tremble in the wind

explanation.definitionFit: A young sheep's tail is a woolly extremity that waggles, and hazel catkins share the name.

clue.text: Bread used by a solver

definitions.meaning: a shaped mass of baked bread
the idiom 'use your ...' means use your head, from rhyming slang '... of bread' for head

explanation.walkthrough: British rhyming slang gives 'loaf' (of bread) for 'head', so a solver who thinks hard is using their loaf.
explanation.definitionFit: A baked mass of bread, and slang for the head a solver must use.

clue.text: As a rule, mum's the word !

definitions.text: As a rule, mum's the word !

parts.words: As a rule, mum's the word !
parts.note: 'rule' as government and 'mum' as mother: a system where the mother's word is law, not the idiom for keeping quiet

explanation.definitionFit: A society governed by women, where the mother's say is final, is a form of rule by mothers.

clue.text: He's a deep one

parts.note: 'the deep' is a poetic name for the ocean, so a man of the deep is a sailor, not a profound thinker

explanation.definitionFit: A sailor is a man of the ocean, which poets call the deep.

clue.text: Room for a piece intended to be spoken

indicators.note: the words are to be said out loud, so their sound counts rather than their spelling

parts.note: a piece is a part and intended is meant, giving a part meant

explanation.surface: Someone is hunting for lodgings that suit a single chess piece or a written speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be spoken' means the phrase A PART MEANT, from 'a piece intended', is said out loud and sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A flat or a single chamber in a building is a set of rooms or a room for living in.

clue.text: Thirty days hath not this month

definitions.text: Thirty days hath not this month

parts.words: Thirty days hath not this month
parts.note: parodies the rhyme 'Thirty days hath September': the month measured by the moon's cycle lasts about twenty-nine and a half days

explanation.definitionFit: The moon's cycle from new moon to new moon takes about 29.5 days, short of thirty.

clue.text: Retrospective advice to the proverbial sluggard

definitions.meaning: looking backwards, as a heraldic beast with its head turned to look behind
Proverbs 6:6 says 'Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways', so the advice is to consider, or regard, the ant

explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as REGARD ANT: the Book of Proverbs tells the lazy man to consider the ant.
explanation.definitionFit: In heraldry a creature looking back over its shoulder is described with this word, so it means backward-looking.

clue.text: A water-pipe put together at top speed

parts.note: a water main is the principal pipe carrying the supply

explanation.surface: A plumbing job is assembled in a tearing hurry.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic adverb meaning with full force or at full speed.

clue.text: Big bell one takes to the Duce

parts.note: Big Ben is the great bell in the clock tower at Westminster
I is the Roman numeral for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: A huge bell is carried off to Mussolini.
explanation.walkthrough: Big Ben is the great bell of the clock tower of London's Houses of Parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: Il Duce was the title of the Italian dictator Mussolini, whose first name this is.

clue.text: Architect's support — one in place of a broken leg ?

indicators.note: one piece goes in the other, set within its letters

parts.note: a broken leg is set in a plaster cast
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An architect wonders if a cast could stand in for a fractured limb.
explanation.definitionFit: A rectangular column projecting from a wall gives an architect a supporting feature.

clue.text: Fondness for legal seizure ?

definitions.meaning: affection or a strong liking for someone
taking property into custody by court order to satisfy a debt

explanation.definitionFit: A bond of affection, and the legal seizing of goods or earnings by a court.

clue.text: A growth of religion, Holmes's last occupation?

parts.note: PI, short for pious, is the crossword sense of religious
a culture is a growth of cells or bacteria

explanation.surface: A new sect springs up, prompting a question about the great detective's final career.
explanation.walkthrough: In Conan Doyle's stories Sherlock Holmes retires to the Sussex Downs to keep bees.
explanation.definitionFit: Sherlock Holmes spent his retirement beekeeping, the craft of raising bees.

clue.text: Cut across its centre perhaps

parts.note: two lines crossing at a midpoint meet and divide each other

explanation.definitionFit: Two lines that cross each other at a midpoint meet and divide each other.

clue.text: But a candidate must stand to win it

definitions.text: But a candidate must stand to win it

parts.words: But a candidate must stand to win it
parts.note: an election candidate stands for a parliamentary place, though the prize is something to sit on

explanation.definitionFit: A place in parliament is won by standing for election, yet it is a chair.

clue.text: Hellish long fork ?

parts.note: a devil torturing souls with a pitchfork, and also the name of a long-handled cook's fork used at sea

explanation.definitionFit: A fiend who torments, and a long toasting fork used by a ship's cook, share the name.

clue.text: Christ College, Cambridge

definitions.meaning: a name for the Messiah meaning 'God with us'
a college of Cambridge University founded in 1584

explanation.walkthrough: 'Christ College, Cambridge' looks like one name (there is a Christ's College); split it into the Messiah and a different Cambridge college.
explanation.definitionFit: A title for the Messiah from Isaiah, and a college of Cambridge University.

clue.text: Do the heartless lovers do so ?

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the word without its heart keeps only its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A riddle asks whether the cruel and unfeeling are capable of love.
explanation.definitionFit: Lovers are besotted, lavishing excessive fondness on their beloved.

clue.text: It measures the dive with which a baseball player gets round home

indicators.note: one word surrounds the other, its letters placed around it

parts.note: the batter is the player at the plate in baseball
taken as written

explanation.surface: A baseball hitter dives at home plate while something records the plunge.
explanation.definitionFit: A device for gauging the depth of water, measuring how deep a dive goes.

clue.text: Plight of an onion ?

parts.note: an onion preserved in vinegar is in a jar of preserve, which is also an idiom for a sorry plight

explanation.definitionFit: A predicament, and the vinegar preserve in which onions are steeped.

clue.text: The once-rich, ruined the French way …

indicators.note: something ruined is wrecked, so these letters are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: A formerly wealthy family is brought low in the French manner.
explanation.definitionFit: A coastal road cut into a cliff, a French word for a kind of road.

clue.text: Made from the pitch-pine trunk, no doubt

definitions.text: Made from the pitch-pine trunk, no doubt

parts.words: Made from the pitch-pine trunk, no doubt
parts.note: a pine trunk that is pitched, thrown end over end at Highland games

explanation.walkthrough: 'pitch' suggests the resinous pitch-pine; read it as a verb, to toss, as in the Scottish trunk-throwing event.
explanation.definitionFit: The heavy pole tossed in Scottish Highland games is a trimmed tree trunk.

clue.text: … by driving on this side? Tactless!

definitions.meaning: the left, the French word for which is the answer

explanation.walkthrough: The clue continues from 22: in France one drives on the right, so driving on the left would be both the wrong side and gauche, the French for left.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word for left also means socially awkward in English.

clue.text: The looking-glass game

parts.note: Lewis Carroll's Through the Looking-Glass is plotted as a game played on a board of squares

explanation.definitionFit: Through the Looking-Glass follows Alice as a pawn across a chessboard to become a queen.

clue.text: Spike makes a dog mad

indicators.note: a mad arrangement is crazy, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Something sharp drives a hound wild.
explanation.definitionFit: A pointed stick for driving cattle, a prod or spur.

clue.text: Magistrate takes in money from literary house

indicators.note: one piece takes the other into its middle

parts.note: beak is British slang for a magistrate
L is the abbreviation for pound, British money

explanation.surface: A judge accepts cash from someone at a publishing house.
explanation.walkthrough: Bleak House is a Dickens novel; 'beak' is old British slang for a magistrate.
explanation.definitionFit: Bleak House, the title of Dickens's novel, names a fictional residence.

clue.text: Reward for backing volume about luminous flux unit

indicators.note: one piece sits around the other, wrapped about it
the book is read backwards, as if going in reverse

parts.note: a tome is a large book or volume
the lumen is the SI unit of luminous flux

explanation.surface: A scientist is paid for championing a big book on light measurement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns TOME into EMOT, which goes 'about' LUMEN.
explanation.definitionFit: A salary or fee is payment received for work.

clue.text: Retired, stood again ?

definitions.meaning: to stand someone a drink is to treat them, so standing again is treating again

explanation.walkthrough: Split as RE-TREATED: 'stood' is the pub sense of buying a round, not standing up.
explanation.definitionFit: Fell back or withdrew, and also treated once more.

clue.text: The winner, if roles were changed

definitions.text: The winner, if roles were changed

indicators.note: letters that were changed have been moved about, so this word is rearranged

explanation.surface: A sporting result would be reversed if the competitors swapped places.
explanation.walkthrough: As a whole the clue says the beaten one would have won with positions swapped; 'were changed' also rearranges ROLES.
explanation.definitionFit: Reverse the outcome and the victor becomes the one who was beaten.
